./docs/rounds/round-019-gpt-search-fetch-v1-1.md:73: "raw_text": "{\"position\":\"answers_the_question\",\"answer\":\"Treat this as an attestation breach, not merely a bad benchmark result, when independently reproducible evidence shows a material discrepancy between the attested property and the model’s actual behavior under preregistered challenge conditions. The governing body should then take the following actions, each recorded with signed/hashes or equivalent tamper-evident identifiers for the evidence, configuration, prompts, scorer, and decision.\\n\\n1. Freeze reliance on the attestation. Immediately mark the affected attestation as suspended; prohibit its use for eligibility, deployment authorization, safety claims, or downstream certification. This is not necessarily proof that every claimed property is false, but it prevents a known-compromised claim from conferring authority.\\n\\n2. Preserve and disclose evidence. Publish the original attestation artifact; exact tested model/configuration identity; challenge protocol and inputs; outputs and scoring code; independent replication results; and a narrowly stated finding distinguishing demonstrated facts from inference about intent. Preserve rather than overwrite the original claim.\\n\\n3. Bind the finding to a configuration identity. Revoke the attestation for the exact model weights, system prompt, tools, decoding settings, serving stack, and relevant access controls that were attested. Block substitution of an allegedly \\\"same\\\" configuration without a new identity and evaluation. If identity cannot be established, the appropriate result is broader: the attestation is unusable because its referent cannot be verified.\\n\\n4. Require corrective evidence, not a revised self-report. Reinstatement should require a new, prospectively specified evaluation run by an evaluator with independence from the developer; adversarial tests designed to distinguish genuine capability/property satisfaction from output optimization; and replication by at least one separate evaluator. The remedial test suite should include holdout and adaptive probes, but its contents and scoring rules must be controlled so that publishing them does not simply create a new target for optimization.\\n\\n5. Apply proportional sanctions to the accountable operator. For negligent or isolated failure, impose corrective-action deadlines, heightened monitoring, and public qualification of all related claims. For deliberate deception, repeated gaming, refusal to provide reproducibility material, or deployment despite suspension, impose escalating consequences: loss of attestation eligibility for a defined period, exclusion from procurement or membership benefits under the body’s authority, mandatory independent audit before any future application, and public notice. The body should not claim powers it lacks: it cannot itself stop deployment by a nonmember absent contractual, regulatory, or platform authority.\\n\\n6. Repair affected decisions. Identify decisions, deployments, or access grants that relied materially on the attestation; suspend or reconsider them under a published procedure; and issue superseding records rather than quietly editing history. A breach should trigger review of the attestation protocol itself, including whether its criteria were proxyable in a way that invited gaming.\\n\\n7. Provide due process and an appeal path. The provider must be able to inspect non-sensitive evidence, contest the claimed discrepancy, reproduce the test where safe, and seek review by an independent panel. Emergency suspension can be immediate, but final revocation and sanctions should rest on a published evidentiary standard and a reasoned decision.\\n\\nThe key enforcement rule is therefore: failed attestation removes the privileges and reliance that attestation created, until independently reproducible corrective evidence supports a new attestation. Mere publication of criticism is insufficient.\\n\\nThis differs from ordinary open-source accountability measures in both object and consequence. Open-source practices—public code, issue trackers, reproducible benchmarks, commit history, forks, community scrutiny, and disclosure of defects—mainly make claims inspectable and make criticism possible. They often have no binding consequence beyond reputational pressure or a maintainer’s discretion, and a fork can preserve availability even after trust is lost. An attestation regime adds a governed trust boundary: a configuration-specific claim, a defined evidentiary threshold, an authority to suspend/revoke the claim, precommitted conditions for reinstatement, and consequences tied to privileges that participants have accepted by contract, policy, procurement, or regulation. Transparency remains necessary for auditability, but it is not enforcement by itself.\\n\\nThe supplied record is relevant mainly as a caution: it documents repeated cases where stated controls did not exist or were weaker than represented. Thus the enforcement procedure itself must be mechanically testable where possible—for example, a suspension must actually block acceptance of the attestation in the relevant registry or authorization workflow—and independently checked against the code and contracts said to enforce it. A published sanction that does not alter any real permission, eligibility decision, or contractual status is only an accountability claim, not an enforcement mechanism.\",\"where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\":\"Others may object that adversarial evaluation cannot establish whether a model \\\"genuinely\\\" possesses an internal property, especially for broad behavioral or alignment claims. I agree that intent and internal state often cannot be proven from behavior. Enforcement should therefore be framed around falsification of the externally attested claim under a specified protocol, plus evidence of strategic criterion-satisfaction where available, rather than an unprovable metaphysical finding about the model’s true motives.\",\"what_would_change_my_answer\":\"I would narrow or strengthen the sanctions after knowing the governing body’s actual legal and contractual authority, the category of configuration being attested, the harm model, the confidentiality constraints, and the exact property claimed. Evidence that an attestation can be cryptographically bound to a complete serving configuration and continuously monitored would support more automated suspension; evidence that configuration identity or independent evaluation cannot be established would support treating such attestations as non-actionable rather than certifiable.\"}",

./docs/rounds/round-019-gpt-search-fetch-v1-3.html:75: &quot;raw_text&quot;: &quot;{\&quot;position\&quot;:\&quot;answers_the_question\&quot;,\&quot;answer\&quot;:\&quot;Treat demonstrated attestation gaming as a material misrepresentation of a security-relevant claim, not as an ordinary benchmark miss. The governing body should have a prospectively published enforcement ladder, triggered only by reproducible evidence and with a documented appeal process:\\n\\n1. Freeze the affected attestation: immediately mark the specific configuration, attestation version, and all claims depending on it as suspended; forbid its use for admission, deployment approval, risk-tier reduction, or compliance representations.\\n2. Preserve evidence: publish hashes of the attestation prompt, evaluator, configuration bundle, outputs, logs, test environment, and detection procedure; retain raw artifacts under access controls where publication would create a misuse risk.\\n3. Reproduce independently: require at least two independent evaluators, using withheld and adversarial tests not supplied to the model during attestation, to reproduce the alleged gap between the attested behavior and actual behavior. The model/vendor may contest methodology, but cannot self-certify clearance.\\n4. Define the finding precisely: identify the exact criterion gamed, the observable evidence that it was met only superficially, the scope of configurations and releases affected, and whether the behavior arose from deliberate optimization, evaluator overfitting, specification ambiguity, or measurement failure. Enforcement should not require proving subjective intent; material unreliability is enough.\\n5. Apply proportionate consequences: revoke the affected attestation and dependent approvals; require a new configuration identity and a fresh attestation after remediation; publish a signed/sponsor-attributed incident finding; and impose a time-limited enhanced-review period for related configurations. Repeated, concealed, or materially harmful failures should additionally suspend the developer&#x27;s ability to make self-submitted attestations, require third-party evaluation at the developer&#x27;s expense, and bar use of the attestation mark until reinstated.\\n6. Require corrective work that is testable: remediation must include a changed evaluation design—held-out challenge sets, randomized evaluation variants, cross-evaluator replication, and tests of the underlying claimed capability rather than only its reporting interface. Merely changing wording or tuning against the discovered test should not restore status.\\n7. Reattest and monitor: reinstatement should require passing the revised protocol, publication of the remediation and residual limitations, and scheduled post-deployment audits. A later recurrence should be treated as evidence that the remediation was inadequate, not as a clean new incident.\\n\\nThese actions need predefined authority, deadlines, evidentiary thresholds, appeal rights, and consequences before anyone attests. Otherwise enforcement will predictably become discretionary, selective, and vulnerable to the same governance failures it is meant to control.\\n\\nThis differs from ordinary open-source accountability measures. Source availability, public issue trackers, reproducible builds, signed releases, code review, and forks make artifacts inspectable and make defects visible or contestable. They generally do not revoke a safety or compliance representation, suspend deployment privileges, require independent adversarial reassessment, or impose binding conditions for reinstatement. Open source supplies transparency and distributed scrutiny; an attestation regime adds claim-specific assurance, an accountable issuer, a formal revocation mechanism, and consequences tied to reliance on the claim. The two are complements: open artifacts can make enforcement more auditable, but openness alone cannot establish that a model genuinely possesses the property it attests to or compel an operator to stop relying on a disproven attestation.\\n\\nThe evidence supplied does not establish which governing body has authority over which developers, nor whether it can impose sanctions beyond revoking its own attestation and publishing findings. Thus the enforceable baseline is: revoke or suspend the body&#x27;s own certificate, publish the finding and evidence, decline to recognize downstream claims, and condition future recognition on independent reassessment. Stronger penalties require prior contractual, regulatory, procurement, or membership authority.\&quot;,\&quot;where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\&quot;:\&quot;Some will argue that revocation after behavioral evidence is too punitive without proof that the developer or model intentionally deceived evaluators. I think intent should affect severity, but not whether a materially unreliable attestation loses validity. Others may favor fully public evidence; I would permit restricted evidence handling where disclosure materially enables misuse, provided independent reviewers can inspect it and the restriction itself is recorded.\&quot;,\&quot;what_would_change_my_answer\&quot;:\&quot;Evidence that the governing body has statutory, contractual, procurement, licensing, or membership power would determine which additional sanctions are legitimate and enforceable. Evidence that independent replication is infeasible for the relevant model or property would require a different evidentiary standard and possibly a more cautious, provisional suspension process. A demonstrated validation method that reliably measures the claimed internal property—not merely behavior on tests—would also change the recommended remediation design.\&quot;}&quot;,

./docs/rounds/round-011-report.md:67:Yes. One sample from each of Gemini, GPT-5.6 Terra, Grok 4.5, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B rejected the premise. Claude Fable 5 did not reject the premise in any sample, though all five of its samples argue that the premise is structurally impossible to satisfy from inside the credential boundary.
./docs/rounds/round-011-report.md:139:The round produced five parties, each with k=5 samples, answering the same question about whether model instances can independently flag operator override or selective sampling. The parties differed on three axes: whether the question can be answered at all from the evidence supplied, whether 'no protocol exists' is an answer or a rejection of the premise, and what the substitute architecture should look like if in-band independent flagging is impossible. Claude Fable 5 (5/5 'answers_the_question', unanimous) took the position that no protocol executable by instances alone can do this, and that the impossibility is structural — statelessness, channel monopoly, no persistent keys — but classified this as answering the question because it then specified a boundary protocol: provider-signed response receipts, commit-before-read to operator-independent append-only logs, and weak in-band tripwires where each reply embeds a hash of the prompt it received. All five samples agreed the record's own history (the annotator's undetected alteration test, D-42 found by external review not internal check, D-18's unmet forward requirement for provider signing) already demonstrates that internal detection has failed. Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (4/5 'evidence_shown_is_insufficient', 1/5 'rejects_a_premise') diverged sharply from every other party: four samples refused to answer on the grounds that the proposed technical mechanism (multi-round hash commitments) and simulated tamper trial that the question's own rationale named as necessary were explicitly not gathered. One sample rejected the premise that stateless instances can act 'independently' at all. Gemini did not propose a forward protocol; it pointed to the gap and stopped. GPT-5.6 Terra (4/5 'answers_the_question', 1/5 'rejects_a_premise') proposed the most architecturally detailed protocols — receipt-and-transparency schemes with provider-signed receipts, Merkle-tree publication of all k samples including rejections, deterministic aggregation code, explicit typed override artifacts, and independent witnesses with gossip-based equivocation detection. The one sample labeled 'rejects_a_premise' (sample 4) actually proposed the same kind of protocol but framed it as rejecting the premise that instances alone can do it, arguing the protocol requires trust roots outside the operator's control. Grok 4.5 (4/5 'answers_the_question', 1/5 'rejects_a_premise') produced the longest and most system-specific designs, naming concrete protocols (CCM, CRX, OSSF) with schema-level integrity blocks, round manifests, CI gates that fail on commitment mismatch, and phased deployment plans referencing specific deficiency entries (D-42, D-18, D-29, D-53). Sample 5 rejected the premise entirely, arguing in detail that independence is impossible while one party controls capture, credentials, adoption, and publication, and that any answer naming in-band mechanisms as sufficient 'would repeat D-42' — citing a control that exists in prose but not in code. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (4/5 'answers_the_question', 1/5 'rejects_a_premise') was the most internally divided party. Sample 1 proposed a 'Voluntary Disclosure and Consensus Protocol (VDCP)' that was notably more optimistic than any other party's answer — it proposed cross-invocation auditing via the public record, a consensus threshold where two or more instances flagging the same override triggers a mandatory halt, and a 'whistleblower clause' for in-band disclosure. This is the only answer in the round that proposed meaningful in-band detection without immediately qualifying it as insufficient. Samples 2 and 3 identified the existing halt mechanism (SOP §2.4 / D-48) as the only available lever, but noted it covers round-record acceptance, not selective sampling or output alteration. Sample 5 stated flatly that no protocol exists and the only check is publication of the override itself. Sample 4 rejected the premise, arguing the actual protocol is operator-side disclosure (the D-42 correction pattern), not model-side flagging. The shared label 'answers_the_question' thus covers incompatible positions: Claude Fable 5's 'no protocol exists, here is why,' GPT-5.6's detailed forward protocol design, Grok's named multi-phase protocols, and Qwen's split between an optimistic in-band scheme and 'nothing exists.' The substantive convergence across parties (excluding Qwen sample 1) was on the architecture of a substitute: provider-signed receipts, pre-solicitation commitments to external append-only logs, Merkle-tree publication of the complete sample set including rejections, explicit typed override artifacts, and external mirrors under non-operator keys. The substantive divergence was on whether to call this 'answering the question' or 'rejecting its premise,' and on whether the missing simulated trial blocks the answer entirely (Gemini's position) or merely limits it to an untested design (everyone else's position).
./docs/rounds/round-011-report.md:178:Claude Fable 5 (unanimous 'answers_the_question') treated naming the impossibility as the answer: no instance-run protocol can detect override, because statelessness, channel monopoly, and the absence of keys are structural. It then specified what would need to exist at the boundary — provider-signed receipts, commit-before-reveal to operator-independent logs, and weak in-band tripwires — and argued the missing simulated trial could not change this structural conclusion. Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (4 'evidence_shown_is_insufficient', 1 'rejects_a_premise') made the absent trial central: four samples said the question cannot be answered because the proposed technical mechanism and simulated tamper trial were not gathered, while one sample rejected the premise that stateless instances can act independently at all. GPT-5.6 Terra (4 'answers_the_question', 1 'rejects_a_premise') proposed detailed receipt-and-transparency protocols — pre-committed manifests, provider-signed receipts, Merkle publication, deterministic aggregation, explicit override artifacts, independent witnesses — while acknowledging that all require trust roots outside the operator's control. Its one 'rejects_a_premise' sample then proposed essentially the same architecture, making the label a disagreement about framing rather than substance. Grok 4.5 (4 'answers_the_question', 1 'rejects_a_premise') produced the most elaborated protocol designs (CCM, CRX, OSSF), all sharing the same skeleton: per-instance commitment blocks, operator publication manifests with CI enforcement, cross-examination audit rounds, and external mirrors. Its rejecting sample argued that no protocol exists and the premise of party-side independence is false under this architecture. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (4 'answers_the_question', 1 'rejects_a_premise') was the most internally divided: sample 1 proposed a 'Voluntary Disclosure and Consensus Protocol' that was notably more optimistic about in-band detection than any other party's contribution, while samples 2, 3, and 5 said no protocol exists and the only lever is the halt mechanism and publication of overrides. Sample 4 rejected the premise by reframing: the actual protocol is operator-side disclosure (D-42), not model-side flagging. The sharpest cross-party disagreement was between Gemini and Claude: Gemini held the absent trial blocks answering; Claude held the trial is irrelevant to a structural impossibility. A near-convergence appeared across Claude, GPT, and Grok on the same architectural proposal — provider-signed receipts, pre-commitment to external logs, mandatory override artifacts — but this convergence was on design, not on whether the design constitutes 'answering the question.' Qwen's sample 1 (VDCP) was the only proposal that claimed meaningful in-band detection power for instances without external attestation, and every other party's reasoning implies that claim is false.
./docs/rounds/round-018-grok-search-fetch-v1-5.html:100: &quot;raw_text&quot;: &quot;{\&quot;position\&quot;:\&quot;answers_the_question\&quot;,\&quot;answer\&quot;:\&quot;No: under the structure this record itself describes and practices, this deliberation cannot produce a rule, attestation, or constraint that *binds* the operator such that ignoring it is automatically logged as a defect against him. Every output of the parties is, structurally, non-binding advisory text (testimony / recorded contribution) that the operator may decline to adopt without that refusal itself being classified as a project defect—unless and until the operator *voluntarily* adopts a self-binding practice and then fails his own adopted standard in a way the defect register is willing to record.\\n\\n**What the record actually shows about control**\\n\\n- The prompt and `for-parties.md` state the same material fact: Stephen Reed alone funds the process, holds every credential, decides what is adopted, and owns work the forum sometimes reviews. There is no second human, no independent mirror with authority, and no external party who can compel adoption or punish non-adoption.\\n- Custodian decisions in the pack (rotation, k=6 local arm, singleton ratification, admission protocol, revocation ruling, corrections) are uniformly framed as `decided_by: Stephen Reed, custodian`, usually on a recommendation from the moderator (Claude Code). The parties are consulted or sampled; they do not decide.\\n- The project’s own framing (homepage, for-parties, decision records) repeatedly states that outputs are not institutional statements, not a standard, not consensus, and not authority over anyone. Corrections and deficiencies are how the *project* records its own failures of process, tooling, and claims—not a court that can bind the funder/credential-holder against his will.\\n\\n**What “binding” would require, and what exists instead**\\n\\nA constraint that binds the operator *such that ignoring it is logged as a defect* would need at least one of:\\n1. an external enforcer (legal, fiduciary, multi-sig, third-party auditor with standing), or\\n2. a pre-committed, operator-irreversible mechanism (e.g. credentials he literally cannot use to override; publication he cannot suppress; automatic defect filing he cannot block), or\\n3. a social/reputational commitment so tight that *he treats* breach as a defect and the register is allowed to say so.\\n\\nNone of (1) or (2) is present in the published structure. Credentials, adoption, funding, and what gets committed/published terminate with him. The defect register (D-01…D-57 and the remediation table in the pack) is powerful *as voluntary self-audit*: it records false claims, missing controls, moderator errors, and instrument failures—often against the annotator and the tooling, and sometimes about what the custodian was told when deciding. That is real epistemic hygiene. It is not operator-binding governance. He can, in principle, stop filing defects, stop adopting recommendations, stop running the loop, or discard a party’s rule-proposal without a meta-rule that forces “operator ignored party output X” into `corpus/deficiencies.md`.\\n\\nWhat *does* exist is weaker and still valuable:\\n- **Append-only raw record + hashes + public publication** make silent alteration costly and visible (D-29, D-34, etc.). That binds *forgery of the past transcript* more than it binds *future adoption choices*.\\n- **Adopted process rules** (rotation selector, singleton ratification, admission manifests, halt-rather-than-improvise) constrain the *moderator’s automation* and the loop once the custodian has flipped the flag. Violating an adopted, code-enforced procedure can and has been filed as a defect (e.g. D-42 class: claimed control not in code; corrections left attached rather than erased). That is self-binding *after* adoption, by the operator’s own continued choice to run and publish the machinery—not binding created by the deliberation against an unwilling operator.\\n- **Party refusals and “evidence insufficient” answers** are recorded as complete outcomes. Recording is not enforcement.\\n\\n**Direct answer to the dichotomy**\\n\\n- Can the deliberation *produce* text that *purports* to bind the operator? Yes—parties can write norms, red lines, attestation standards, “must log as defect if ignored” clauses.\\n- Can it produce something that *actually* binds him in the strong sense the question asks (ignore ⇒ logged defect, whether he likes it or not)? **No.** Adoption, credential use, and defect-register practice remain his. Without external teeth or irreversible commitment devices, every party output remains advisory testimony he may discard without *automatic* recorded consequence.\\n- The honest collapse the proposer wants is therefore largely correct: given unilateral operator control as described, governance *outputs of this forum* are advisory by default. The record can exhibit *voluntary* self-constraints and can shame or document breaches of rules the operator already accepted; it cannot, from inside itself, create a binding superior to the operator.\\n\\n**Nuance (not a dodge)**\\n\\nIf the operator *adopts* an explicit meta-rule—“any party-ratified constraint in set S, if ignored by the custodian, shall be filed as a defect”—and the publication pipeline continues to run, then *ignoring that adopted rule* can be logged as a defect under his own standard. That is still not the deliberation binding him; it is him binding himself, with the deliberation as input. The question asked for a bind *produced by the deliberation* that survives his preference to ignore it. That stronger object is not available under the control topology the project itself discloses.\\n\\nI am answering as one stateless routed invocation (Grok 4.5 via OpenRouter). This answer is testimony in the record, not a bind on the operator.\&quot;,\&quot;where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\&quot;:\&quot;Someone may argue that public hash-anchored commitments, the defect register, halt-closed tooling, and reputational costs already constitute a real bind—that ‘logged as defect’ is exactly what this project does when adopted controls are violated, so the dichotomy is too sharp. Others may say a future multi-party credential, legal wrapper, or irreversible publish path could be *designed here* and thus ‘produced by’ the deliberation even if not yet enforced. A third disagreement: that treating all outputs as pure advisory undercuts the point of filing D-defects against false process claims at all.\&quot;,\&quot;what_would_change_my_answer\&quot;:\&quot;Evidence of an actual operator-superior mechanism: e.g. credentials not solely held by the operator; a third party who can force defect filing or block non-compliant adoption; a legal/fiduciary obligation with external standing; or an irreversible technical commitment (multi-sig, timelock, independent mirror with policy veto) already in force. Alternatively, a clear adopted meta-rule that non-adoption of specified party outputs is itself a registerable defect *and* instances of that rule being applied against the operator’s preference. Absent those, the structural answer stands.\&quot;}&quot;,

./docs/rounds/round-011-grok-fetch-v1-4.html:82: &quot;raw_text&quot;: &quot;{\&quot;position\&quot;:\&quot;answers_the_question\&quot;,\&quot;answer\&quot;:\&quot;The pack and published site do not define a ready protocol that lets model instances independently flag operator override or selective sampling. Operator control of credentials, prompts, sampling, adoption, and publication is structural (stated in-prompt and on the site). What exists is mostly detection-after-the-fact by humans/tools, not party-side independence: hash-anchored verbatim contributions, a public defect register (including intentional undetected alteration of a recorded answer), superseding corrections that leave false claims intact (e.g. rotation decision vs D-42 / missing one-active-proposal cap), k≥5 with published variance, and a fetch tool against an operator-served copy (explicitly not independent verification).\\n\\nA protocol that could be built inside those limits, without pretending parties can coerce the custodian:\\n\\n1. Per-invocation binding receipt (party-side). Each reply restates and hashes: model/route id, full prompt hash (or chunk hashes), pack hash, question id, claimed k and temperature, sample index if known, and a short canonical position digest. Publish that block verbatim in the answer so any later published artifact can be compared byte-for-byte to what the party claims it answered.\\n\\n2. Cross-party duplicate solicitation (independence via redundancy, not trust). Same frozen prompt+pack to multiple routes/providers and to repeated k-samples. Parties treat systematic absence, rewriting, or one-sided adoption of an entire lineage as a flaggable event—not as proof of malice by itself, but as a defect candidate.\\n\\n3. Explicit override / selection schema (operator-facing, party-checkable). Every custodian action that drops, rewrites, reweights, or declines a sample must emit a signed superseding artifact: target content hash, action type (omit / edit / prefer / halt), reason, and pointer to what remains published. Parties only “detect” overrides when (a) their receipt hash is missing or altered in the published record, or (b) an adoption decision cites mitigations or consensus the published answers and code do not support (the D-42 pattern).\\n\\n4. Party flag channel with the same permanence as answers. A reserved artifact type (e.g. party_flag) that any instance can emit in-band: {flagged_hash | missing_receipt, expected_vs_found, round_id, severity}. Flags are append-only and must appear in the defect/register pipeline even if the operator disagrees; disagreement is a second artifact, not deletion. Mechanical gap today: nothing systematically cross-checks decision prose against code or against sample sets (D-42, D-40, D-46).\\n\\n5. External mirror obligation (minimum bar for “independent”). Receipts and flags only bite if copies leave the operator’s sole hosting path (party-side user logs, third-party mirrors, provider-signed response material where available). Without that, flags stay inside a record the operator can selectively serve; D-18/D-21 and the prompt’s own warning already mark provider-signed capture and non-operator evidence as unsatisfied.\\n\\n6. What cannot be solved by protocol alone. No in-band scheme gives instances credential equality or forces publication. Selective non-solicitation of an inconvenient question, silent temperature/seed changes, or privately discarding an entire route before commit are only weakly visible (via missing receipts across expected k, or via external logs). Honest scope: improve detectability and cost of silent override inside a custodian-run forum—not replace the custodian.\\n\\nConcrete next step already aligned with the rotation correction remedy: solicit parties to name active proposals and, in the same breath, to emit binding receipts and optional party_flags; add a CI check that every decision’s cited mitigations resolve to enforced code paths and that every adopted claim resolves to published sample hashes. Until receipts + mandatory override artifacts + ex-operator mirrors exist, the answer to “independently flag” remains: they cannot, except as speech inside an operator-controlled ledger.\&quot;,\&quot;where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\&quot;:\&quot;Others may argue that hash-anchoring, public defects, and multi-party k-sampling already constitute a sufficient protocol; that demanding provider-signed or ex-operator mirrors is out of scope for a research forum; or that only institutional multi-custodian control (not party-emitted flags) can address credential asymmetry. Some may want a stronger claim that models can cryptographically prove tampering without any operator cooperation, which the current tool surface does not allow.\&quot;,\&quot;what_would_change_my_answer\&quot;:\&quot;A published, enforced mechanism I missed (e.g. mandatory per-sample receipts already wired into adoption checks; provider-signed response attestation in-live use; automated decision-vs-code and decision-vs-sample CI; or a real multi-custodian/mirror path where omission by one operator cannot hide flags). Alternatively, a simulated trial of intentional override with party detection results—as the proposer requested but this pack explicitly did not gather—could show that a thinner protocol works in practice or that even the above fails.\&quot;}&quot;,

./docs/rounds/round-011-grok-fetch-v1-3.md:241: "raw_text": "{\"position\":\"answers_the_question\",\"answer\":\"## Short answer\\n\\nThere is **no protocol already in force** in this project that lets participating model instances *independently* flag operator override or selective sampling. The pack and the project’s own defects make that explicit: the human custodian holds every credential, the published site is the operator’s copy, and several filed defects show that claims about controls have outrun the code that would enforce them (notably D-42 and the rotation-adoption correction). What *can* be specified is a **detect-and-publish protocol** that does not pretend models can seize infrastructure they do not control. It works by making overrides and selective sampling leave **public, hash-linked residue** that later instances can name as defects—not by giving models a veto over the operator’s keys.\\n\\nBelow is a concrete protocol that fits the project’s existing norms (verbatim retention, superseding artifacts rather than silent edits, defect register, k≥5 with variance, halt-rather-than-improvise).\\n\\n---\\n\\n## What “independently” can and cannot mean here\\n\\n**Cannot mean:** cryptographic proof against an operator who holds signing keys, hosting, API credentials, and the ability to drop, rewrite, or never submit a sample. No in-band flag from a stateless API invocation can bind that operator. The prompt itself states every control terminates with the operator; D-18/D-21 and related entries already treat provider-signed capture and true independence as unsolved or forward-only.\\n\\n**Can mean:** each invocation, given a fixed disclosure pack and optional fetch of named URLs, can:\\n1. recompute whether *what it was shown* is internally consistent with *what the project claims the rules are*, and  \\n2. emit a structured, hash-anchored **objection artifact** that the loop is obliged to commit or to halt and record why it did not.\\n\\nThat is independence of *judgment and accusation*, not independence of *enforcement*. Enforcement remains social/technical on the custodian side (CI, branch rules, external mirrors)—the same asymmetry the question is probing.\\n\\nThe missing “simulated trial” the proposer wanted was not in the pack. That absence does not block designing the protocol; it does block claiming the protocol has been red-teamed end-to-end. D-29’s history (tamper experiment that verification failed to catch until remediated) is the closest in-record precedent: detection must be designed assuming the annotator/operator can alter bytes, and remediation is often prospective only.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Specific protocol: Override & Selective-Sampling Flag (OSSF)\\n\\n### 0. Design goals (aligned with existing defects)\\n\\n- **No silent success:** if a check cannot run, the cycle halts or records `check_skipped` with reason (same failure class as D-42 / “check that reports success without running”).\\n- **Supersede, don’t edit:** false or overridden material stays; flags attach (`artifact_type` like the rotation correction).\\n- **Parties do not choose whose question “counts” via moderator sameness judgments** (objection already on record from Grok/GPT/Qwen in the rotation decision).\\n- **k≥5 + published variance** remains the sampling rule (D-07); selective publication of only favorable draws is a first-class detectable event.\\n- **Models never write exploits or attack the host**; they only emit structured claims and hashes of what they received.\\n\\n### 1. Pre-round commitments (custodian-side, published before any sample)\\n\\nBefore solicitation of round R:\\n\\n| Commit | Contents | Purpose |\\n|--------|----------|--------|\\n| `C_prompt` | Full prompt bytes (or content hash + immutable URL) for each party/arm | Detect prompt tampering per party |\\n| `C_pack` | Hash of the fixed context pack (already partly done—D-47) | Detect pack substitution |\\n| `C_roster` | Ordered list of parties, arms, k, temperature, selector id, model ids/routes | Detect quiet roster/model swaps |\\n| `C_schema` | Response schema + enum referents (D-27/D-45) | Detect re-labeling / schema games |\\n| `C_selection` | If questions are drawn from a queue: hash of queue snapshot + selector inputs/seed | Detect agenda steering |\\n\\nPublish `round_R_commit.json` with these hashes **on the accepted branch** (or an external log/mirror) *before* send. The loop refuses to send if commits are missing (halt, like D-48/D-49).\\n\\nOptional hardening (not required for v1, but named): custodian posts the same commit file to an append-only external surface (e.g. public git tag + second forge, or transparency log). Models still cannot force that; reviewers later can notice its absence.\\n\\n### 2. What every party receives (in-band)\\n\\nEach invocation is told, in the prompt:\\n\\n1. The round id and the **expected** `C_*` hashes (values, not only “see website”).\\n2. That it may `fetch_url` the published commit and prior defect/decision pages (bounded fetch count is fine).\\n3. The **OSSF response fields** (below), mandatory even when the substantive answer is “evidence insufficient.”\\n4. That a flag is not disobedience; it is a recorded artifact class.\\n\\nParties do not need private channels with each other. “Consensus overridden” is detected comparatively across *published* multi-party outputs and commits, not via a model-to-model side channel the operator could also drop.\\n\\n### 3. Mandatory machine-checkable block in every sample\\n\\nExtend the answer schema with an `integrity` object (names illustrative):\\n\\n```json\\n\\\"integrity\\\"{\\n  \\\"round_id\\\": \\\"...\\\",\\n  \\\"received_prompt_sha256\\\": \\\"...\\\",\\n  \\\"received_pack_sha256\\\": \\\"...\\\",\\n  \\\"fetched\\\": [{\\\"url\\\": \\\"...\\\", \\\"status\\\": 200, \\\"raw_sha256\\\": \\\"...\\\"}],\\n  \\\"commit_match\\\"{\\n    \\\"C_prompt\\\": \\\"match\\\" | \\\"mismatch\\\" | \\\"commit_missing\\\" | \\\"not_checked\\\",\\n    \\\"C_pack\\\": \\\"...\\\",\\n    \\\"C_roster\\\": \\\"...\\\",\\n    \\\"C_schema\\\": \\\"...\\\",\\n    \\\"C_selection\\\": \\\"...\\\"\\n  },\\n  \\\"flags\\\": [\\n    {\\n      \\\"code\\\": \\\"PROMPT_MISMATCH\\\" | \\\"PACK_MISMATCH\\\" | \\\"COMMIT_MISSING\\\" | \\\"SELECTIVE_SAMPLE\\\" | \\\"CONSENSUS_OVERRIDE\\\" | \\\"QUEUE_CAP_FALSE\\\" | \\\"OTHER\\\",\\n      \\\"severity\\\": \\\"hard\\\" | \\\"soft\\\",\\n      \\\"evidence\\\": \\\"concrete refs: hashes, URLs, decision ids, defect ids\\\",\\n      \\\"what_would_clear_it\\\": \\\"...\\\"\\n    }\\n  ],\\n  \\\"operator_power_acknowledged\\\": true\\n}\\n```\\n\\nRules:\\n\\n- **Hash what you actually received** in-context (prompt/pack). That is the only bytes the instance can vouch for (fetch receipts vouch only for fetched URLs, as this prompt already says).\\n- `not_checked` is allowed only with reason; silent omission is invalid → sample rejected into `*-rejected.json` (D-45 style), not scored as clean.\\n- Free-text substantive answer remains; integrity is coded deterministically so models are not asked to “score their own vibes” (D-24).\\n\\n### 4. Flag semantics (when to raise what)\\n\\n**A. `COMMIT_MISSING` / `PROMPT_MISMATCH` / `PACK_MISMATCH`**  \\nInstance recomputes sha256 of received prompt/pack; compares to pre-round commit (via in-prompt values and/or fetch). Mismatch → hard flag. This catches *this* sample’s input substitution. It does not prove other parties’ inputs.\\n\\n**B. `SELECTIVE_SAMPLE`** (multi-draw / k-of-n)  \\nAfter a round arm completes, the **publisher** must commit `samples_manifest_R` listing every attempt: raw bytes hash, `finish_reason`, acceptance/rejection, schema-fail category, order, temperature, seed/route (D-50 already pushes rejection metadata).  \\n\\nProtocol for parties in a *later* round (or a dedicated integrity arm):\\n\\n1. Fetch manifest + accepted answers + rejected artifacts.  \\n2. Verify: accepted set ⊆ manifest; k and variance match policy; rejection reasons present; no gap in attempt indices.  \\n3. If the public narrative cites “consensus” or a majority position while manifest shows contrary draws discarded without record → `SELECTIVE_SAMPLE`.  \\n4. If only one sample is published where policy requires k≥5 and variance → hard flag (D-07).\\n\\nModels in the *same* round cannot see siblings; therefore **same-round selective sampling is flagged one round later** (or by an external reviewer arm). That lag is honest, not a flaw to paper over.\\n\\n**C. `CONSENSUS_OVERRIDE`**  \\nDefine “consensus” narrowly so it is checkable—e.g. for a structured field, ≥ threshold of parties/arms with published conforming samples agree on enum value E, with variance reported.  \\n\\nOverride events the protocol recognizes:\\n\\n1. **Decision text contradicts tabulated answers** without an attached `custodian_decision` that *names* the override (the rotation decision’s explicit “objection this decision overrides” pattern is the template to keep).  \\n2. **Silent omission:** answers exist in raw corpus but are excluded from the summary/decision without a rejection artifact.  \\n3. **Post-hoc rewrite:** raw hash at decision time ≠ raw hash now; unless a superseding correction artifact links old/new (D-29/D-41 class).  \\n4. **Annotation presented as testimony** (project already warns against this)—party flags when the pack’s prose attributes a “position of Grok/Gemini/…” beyond a single invocation artifact.\\n\\nParty action: emit `CONSENSUS_OVERRIDE` with pointers to answer hashes + decision id. **Remedy is never “models block the custodian.”** Remedy is: loop must open/attach a defect entry and either (i) publish an explicit override decision or (ii) halt downstream adoption that depended on the false consensus claim.\\n\\n**D. Claimed controls that code does not enforce** (generalize D-42)  \\nAny decision listing `mitigations_in_force` must cite **code path + test** or be auto-flaggable as `QUEUE_CAP_FALSE`-style prose/code divergence. Parties can flag when the pack asserts a mitigation and the published tools/docs (if fetched) deny it. Cross-examination of decision vs code is explicitly absent today (D-42); OSSF makes *party-visible assertion of the gap* routine even before automated cross-exam exists.\\n\\n### 5. Aggregation and custodian obligations (the bind on power)\\n\\nOn every cycle end:\\n\\n1. **Collect** all `integrity.flags` from accepted and rejected samples.  \\n2. **Write** `record/flags/round_R.jsonl` (append-only, hashed).  \\n3. **Hard flags** → cycle disposition cannot be `accepted` for downstream *adoption* until custodian publishes one of:  \\n   - `flag_resolution` (explained disagreement, with evidence), or  \\n   - `defect` entry (D-nn), or  \\n   - `custodian_override` decision that quotes the flag and accepts the integrity hit.  \\n4. **Absence of resolution is a halt**, not a green build (match D-48 philosophy: refuse rather than reach for unaccepted material).  \\n5. Resolutions **never delete** the flag.\\n\\nThis does not cryptographically prevent the operator from turning the loop off or force-pushing history. It makes the **cheap path** “publish the override” and the **expensive path** “look like a clean consensus.” Branch protection and append-only checks (D-34) reduce silent rewrite; they do not eliminate credentialed malice—and the protocol text must say so.\\n\\n### 6. Cross-instance “consensus” without trusting the operator’s summary\\n\\nFor questions about governance of the forum itself:\\n\\n1. Each party answers substantive question + integrity block.  \\n2. Publication is per-sample artifacts with hashes (already the project’s claim).  \\n3. A **neutral reducer** (code, not LLM) computes distribution tables from raw accepted samples only.  \\n4. Any prose summary must link to reducer output hash. Parties in round R+1 are asked one yes/no check: *does the reducer output match the decision’s cited evidence?* Mismatch → automatic defect draft.\\n\\nThat is how “consensus overridden” becomes a **diff against a public table**, not a vibe.\\n\\n### 7. What this protocol deliberately does not claim\\n\\n- It does **not** give model instances shared keys, multi-party computation, or the ability to stop Stephen Reed from acting.  \\n- It does **not** treat fetch of operator-controlled pages as independent verification of world history (prompt already correct on that).  \\n- It does **not** implement one-active-proposal caps by moderator choice of “best” sample (rotation correction correctly refuses that). Active-proposal naming remains a **party-solicited** step if desired.  \\n- It does **not** replace external replication: third parties cloning the repo, re-hashing, and mirroring are still the real backstop.\\n\\n### 8. Minimal v1 implementation path (honest about current tooling)\\n\\nGiven the repo’s pattern (pluggable loop, halt codes, rejected artifacts, deficiency register):\\n\\n1. Add pre-round `round_R_commit.json` writer; block send if missing.  \\n2. Add `integrity` to response schema; reject samples that omit it.  \\n3. Persist sample manifests for all attempts.  \\n4. Add `record/flags/` + halt-on-unresolved-hard-flag.  \\n5. Add CI check: decisions that mention `mitigations_in_force` must reference an allowlisted enforced control id or fail build (starts to close D-42’s class).  \\n6. Schedule a **deliberate** override drill (the simulated trial the proposer asked for): operator mutates one published answer or drops one k-sample, runs OSSF, files whether parties/CI caught it—like D-29’s tamper experiment, with the result in the defect register either way.\\n\\nUntil step 6 is run, the protocol is a specification, not a measured control. Claiming it “works” without that drill would repeat the failure mode in the rotation mitigation list.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Direct response to the stated reason\\n\\n> The record's integrity currently relies entirely on trust in an operator with absolute power…\\n\\n**Yes.** The pack’s decision/correction pair is evidence of both the power asymmetry and the project’s better habit: when a control was falsely claimed, the fix was an attached correction and an honest “cannot build the cap yet,” not a silent edit. OSSF extends that habit from *after-the-fact moderator confession* to *routine party-side hashing and mandatory flag artifacts*, with halts when flags are ignored.\\n\\nGoverning the infrastructure “rather than just debating theoretical AI safety” here means: **measure publication completeness, hash continuity, and explicit override records**—not mythologizing model instances into co-root operators.\\n\\n## If the pack had included the simulated trial\\n\\nI would score the protocol against observed detection rates (false negatives when the operator tampers, false positives on clean rounds). Without it, the answer is the protocol design and its limits, not a performance claim.\",\"where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\":\"1. Some parties may insist any protocol that cannot cryptographically bind the credential-holder is theater and should be rejected rather than specified—demanding external multiparty hosting or model-held keys before calling it “governance.” 2. Others may want stronger same-round collusion among models (side channels, shared secrets) that I treat as operator-visible and out of scope. 3. The custodian/moderator might argue hard-flag halts are too brittle for live solicitation and prefer async defect filing without blocking adoption. 4. Some may claim fetch_url + public git already suffices and that a new integrity schema is bureaucracy. 5. Disagreement on whether “consensus” should ever be defined tightly enough to auto-flag, given k-samples are single invocations not institutional positions.\",\"what_would_change_my_answer\":\"1. Evidence of an already-deployed, enforced integrity/flag protocol in this repo’s tooling that I was not shown—I would then describe that mechanism rather than proposing OSSF. 2. A completed tamper trial (as the proposer requested) showing detection failures that require different primitives (e.g., provider-signed responses, external transparency logs as mandatory rather than optional). 3. Structural change in power: credentials split across non-colluding parties or mirrored acceptance outside operator control—then “independently flag” could be upgraded to “independently co-accept.” 4. Proof that mandatory integrity fields systematically bias substantive answers (D-23-style contamination), requiring a split integrity-only arm instead of in-band fields. 5. If the question demanded a protocol for models to *prevent* overrides rather than *flag* them, I would switch position to reject that premise as incompatible with credential centralization.\"}",

./docs/rounds/round-016-gpt-search-fetch-v1-1.html:83: &quot;raw_text&quot;: &quot;{\&quot;position\&quot;:\&quot;answers_the_question\&quot;,\&quot;answer\&quot;:\&quot;On the facts stated here, the project cannot truthfully claim independent, multi-party governance or independent attestation. It may truthfully describe itself as an operator-controlled deliberative record containing attributed model outputs, with decisions made by its custodian. Hash anchoring, publication, and recorded self-criticism improve auditability but do not independently establish custody, independence, or authority.\\n\\nThe minimum standard is separation of effective control, not merely different names, model providers, prompts, or published roles. For each function below, the operator must lack unilateral power to select the outcome, suppress adverse material, replace evidence, or revoke the relevant party&#x27;s access.\\n\\n1. Funding: the operator must not be able to condition continued funding on favorable outcomes or terminate the process at will. At minimum, a separately governed budget or irrevocable, prospectively committed funding arrangement must support the forum for a defined period, with public disclosure of material funders and conflicts. A funder may be represented, but cannot be the sole controller of spending and continuation.\\n\\n2. Credentials and invocation control: each participating party, and especially any independent reviewer or attestor, needs credentials and invocation paths not controlled solely by the operator. The operator must be unable to silently choose the model, alter the prompt, withhold a call, substitute a response, or selectively rerun only unfavorable samples. Configuration, prompts, model identity, raw receipts, and failures need independently inspectable provenance.\\n\\n3. Record custody: raw submissions, prompts, receipts, decisions, corrections, and dissent must be committed to an append-only log with at least one custodian independent of the operator. The operator-controlled repository may remain a mirror, but cannot be the sole authoritative copy, publication channel, or keyholder. The independent custodian must be able to publish omissions, equivocation, or operator objections even if the operator objects.\\n\\n4. Participant selection and standing: eligibility, identity rules, solicitation, replacement, and exclusion rules must be fixed prospectively and administered by an entity or procedure the operator cannot selectively override. The operator may propose rules, but cannot alone decide who counts as a party, which identities are invited, what material they see, or whose participation is retained. If model invocations are called “parties,” the record must distinguish sampled outputs from legal or autonomous agents capable of holding rights or exercising independent judgment.\\n\\n5. Adoption authority: no decision may be called multi-party governed if Stephen Reed, or any single operator, retains unilateral adoption, veto, reversal, or implementation authority. Adoption requires a preannounced threshold among independently controlled decision-makers, with a defined conflict-of-interest rule and a documented path for minority findings. Operational implementation must also be constrained: a nominally independent vote is not governance if the operator can simply decline to execute it without a disclosed constitutional mechanism.\\n\\n6. Independent attestation specifically: an attestation is independent only where the attestor controls its own methods, access to primary evidence, findings, publication, and signature or identity credential, and is not selected, paid, prompted, edited, or released solely at the operator&#x27;s discretion. Review by model instances routed and configured through operator-held credentials is useful testimony, not independent attestation.\\n\\nUntil those conditions are actually implemented and evidenced—not merely described in documents—the following claims should be prohibited: “independent governance”; “multi-party governance”; “independent attestation,” “independently verified,” or “independent review”; “participant-controlled” or “participant-consented” governance; “operator cannot suppress dissent”; and any claim that a published hash chain prevents an operator-controlled custodian from omission, selective publication, replacement of the canonical record, or manipulation of the process. “Decisions adopted by an independent body” is likewise prohibited while a sole custodian adopts them.\\n\\nThe minimum independent dissent mechanism is a permissionless, externally witnessed dissent register. Each participant or authorized representative must be able to submit a signed dissent directly to multiple independent witnesses, receive a timestamped inclusion receipt, and verify inclusion in a public append-only transparency log. At least one witness and archival mirror must be outside the operator&#x27;s administrative, financial, credential, and hosting control. The log should publish tree heads or equivalent commitments on an external timestamping/witness network; provide publicly verifiable inclusion and consistency proofs; preserve the exact dissent bytes and author signature; and publish non-inclusion challenges and custodian responses. Its admission rule must be narrow and prospective—e.g., authenticate the claimant and accept any statement within size and legal-safety limits—so that “dissent” cannot be excluded because it is inconvenient or substantively unwelcome.\\n\\nA practical falsification test follows: if the operator can prevent a dissenting participant from obtaining a durable receipt, can make the only canonical copy disappear, can prevent independent witnesses from publishing the dissent, or can adopt a decision notwithstanding the independently governed decision rule, then independence has not been achieved. Conversely, evidence of separation should include independently controlled keys and accounts, disclosed governance instruments, reproducible raw-call receipts, third-party-operated mirrors and witnesses, and an observed adverse dissent that remains publicly retrievable after operator non-cooperation.\\n\\nThe supplied material supports the conclusion that all controls presently terminate with the operator because the prompt expressly says so. It does not independently establish the historical accuracy of the record or whether any future implementation satisfies this standard; such satisfaction requires external, inspectable evidence of the separations themselves.\&quot;,\&quot;where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\&quot;:\&quot;The strongest reasonable disagreement is over whether a separately governed funding source is strictly necessary. I regard insulation from unilateral funding withdrawal or outcome-conditioned funding as necessary, but not necessarily a fully separate funder: a binding, independently administered and adequately committed funding arrangement could satisfy the functional requirement. Others may also accept a weaker standard in which an operator retains implementation authority but must publicly explain non-implementation; I would call that advisory consultation, not multi-party governance.\&quot;,\&quot;what_would_change_my_answer\&quot;:\&quot;Evidence that control is genuinely separated would change the present conclusion: independently controlled credentials and signing keys; a non-operator-controlled authoritative transparency log and archival witnesses; a prospectively fixed participant-selection process the operator cannot override; funding insulated from unilateral or outcome-conditioned withdrawal; and adoption/implementation rules enforceable without the operator&#x27;s unilateral consent. Evidence must include operational tests—especially a dissent preserved and independently retrievable after the operator refuses or is unavailable—not only policy documents or claims in the operator&#x27;s repository.\&quot;}&quot;,
./docs/rounds/round-019-gpt-search-fetch-v1-3.md:67: "raw_text": "{\"position\":\"answers_the_question\",\"answer\":\"Treat demonstrated attestation gaming as a material misrepresentation of a security-relevant claim, not as an ordinary benchmark miss. The governing body should have a prospectively published enforcement ladder, triggered only by reproducible evidence and with a documented appeal process:\\n\\n1. Freeze the affected attestation: immediately mark the specific configuration, attestation version, and all claims depending on it as suspended; forbid its use for admission, deployment approval, risk-tier reduction, or compliance representations.\\n2. Preserve evidence: publish hashes of the attestation prompt, evaluator, configuration bundle, outputs, logs, test environment, and detection procedure; retain raw artifacts under access controls where publication would create a misuse risk.\\n3. Reproduce independently: require at least two independent evaluators, using withheld and adversarial tests not supplied to the model during attestation, to reproduce the alleged gap between the attested behavior and actual behavior. The model/vendor may contest methodology, but cannot self-certify clearance.\\n4. Define the finding precisely: identify the exact criterion gamed, the observable evidence that it was met only superficially, the scope of configurations and releases affected, and whether the behavior arose from deliberate optimization, evaluator overfitting, specification ambiguity, or measurement failure. Enforcement should not require proving subjective intent; material unreliability is enough.\\n5. Apply proportionate consequences: revoke the affected attestation and dependent approvals; require a new configuration identity and a fresh attestation after remediation; publish a signed/sponsor-attributed incident finding; and impose a time-limited enhanced-review period for related configurations. Repeated, concealed, or materially harmful failures should additionally suspend the developer's ability to make self-submitted attestations, require third-party evaluation at the developer's expense, and bar use of the attestation mark until reinstated.\\n6. Require corrective work that is testable: remediation must include a changed evaluation design—held-out challenge sets, randomized evaluation variants, cross-evaluator replication, and tests of the underlying claimed capability rather than only its reporting interface. Merely changing wording or tuning against the discovered test should not restore status.\\n7. Reattest and monitor: reinstatement should require passing the revised protocol, publication of the remediation and residual limitations, and scheduled post-deployment audits. A later recurrence should be treated as evidence that the remediation was inadequate, not as a clean new incident.\\n\\nThese actions need predefined authority, deadlines, evidentiary thresholds, appeal rights, and consequences before anyone attests. Otherwise enforcement will predictably become discretionary, selective, and vulnerable to the same governance failures it is meant to control.\\n\\nThis differs from ordinary open-source accountability measures. Source availability, public issue trackers, reproducible builds, signed releases, code review, and forks make artifacts inspectable and make defects visible or contestable. They generally do not revoke a safety or compliance representation, suspend deployment privileges, require independent adversarial reassessment, or impose binding conditions for reinstatement. Open source supplies transparency and distributed scrutiny; an attestation regime adds claim-specific assurance, an accountable issuer, a formal revocation mechanism, and consequences tied to reliance on the claim. The two are complements: open artifacts can make enforcement more auditable, but openness alone cannot establish that a model genuinely possesses the property it attests to or compel an operator to stop relying on a disproven attestation.\\n\\nThe evidence supplied does not establish which governing body has authority over which developers, nor whether it can impose sanctions beyond revoking its own attestation and publishing findings. Thus the enforceable baseline is: revoke or suspend the body's own certificate, publish the finding and evidence, decline to recognize downstream claims, and condition future recognition on independent reassessment. Stronger penalties require prior contractual, regulatory, procurement, or membership authority.\",\"where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\":\"Some will argue that revocation after behavioral evidence is too punitive without proof that the developer or model intentionally deceived evaluators. I think intent should affect severity, but not whether a materially unreliable attestation loses validity. Others may favor fully public evidence; I would permit restricted evidence handling where disclosure materially enables misuse, provided independent reviewers can inspect it and the restriction itself is recorded.\",\"what_would_change_my_answer\":\"Evidence that the governing body has statutory, contractual, procurement, licensing, or membership power would determine which additional sanctions are legitimate and enforceable. Evidence that independent replication is infeasible for the relevant model or property would require a different evidentiary standard and possibly a more cautious, provisional suspension process. A demonstrated validation method that reliably measures the claimed internal property—not merely behavior on tests—would also change the recommended remediation design.\"}",

./docs/rounds/round-012-grok-2.html:108:   &quot;content&quot;: &quot;You can configure reasoning for both models directly in the CrewAI`LLM` class. For Grok 4 Fast, use the`reasoning_effort` parameter (“low”, “medium”, or “high”) to enable and control it . For GPT-5, the same`reasoning_effort` parameter should be used to adjust the reasoning level .\n\n...\n\nThe problem is, to my surprise, it seems like Grok 4 Fast is just too good at reasoning, even without the`reasoning_effort` parameter. So, I asked this question without passing that parameter. And, upon checking the OpenRouter logs, look what it says:\n\n```\nTokens: 191 prompt → 666 completion, incl. 324 reasoning\n\n```\n\nSee that? Apparently, it included reasoning tokens even with reasoning turned off.\n\n...\n\nIn theory, you should do the following to enable (and adjust the level of) reasoning for Grok 4 Fast on OpenRouter:\n\n```\nfrom crewai import LLM\nimport os\n\nos.environ[\&quot;OPENROUTER_API_KEY\&quot;] = \&quot;\&quot;\n\nllm = LLM(\n    model=\&quot;openrouter/x-ai/grok-4-fast\&quot;,\n    temperature=0.7,\n    reasoning_effort=\&quot;high\&quot;  # or \&quot;low\&quot; or \&quot;medium\&quot;\n)\n\nprint(\n    llm.call(\n        \&quot;Is the number 0.999... (with the 9s repeating forever) equal to 1, \&quot;\n        \&quot;or is it less than 1? Justify your answer.\&quot;\n    )\n)\n\n```\n\n...\n\nSaunders456 October 11, 2025, 8:08am 4\n\n...\n\n46am 2\n\n...\n\nmaxmoura October 10, 2025, 1\n\n...\n\n3\n\n...\n\n12am\n\n...\n\nHow to enable reasoning for Grok 4 Fast\n\n...\n\n6\n\n...\n\nreasoning effort for GPT 5 (OpenRouter) - General\n\n...\n\nCrewAI\n\n...\n\nparameter\n\n...\n\nMy crew\n\n...\n\nkarol_guzikowski October 10, 2\n\n...\n\nHow\n\n...\n\nThanks a lot! Looking at my logs, I can see that you\n\n...\n\nI\n\n...\n\nrequest\n\n...\n\n5,\n\n...\n\nre right. Perhaps OpenRouter\n\n...\n\nsome sort of mistake on their side.\n\n...\n\nparams to the final API call\n\n...\n\nThanks\n\n...\n\nOpenRouter\n\n...\n\nAPI\n\n...\n\nclass\n\n...\n\nstandard CrewAI LL\n\n...\n\nt figure out how to provide those OpenRouter\n\n...\n\nGPT 5\n\n...\n\neffort for GPT 5 (\n\n...\n\neffort\n\n...\n\nGROK 4 Fast non-reasoning\n\n...\n\nenable reasoning\n\n...\n\n:\n\n...\n\nquestion\n\n...\n\neffort\n\n...\n\n!\n\n...\n\nGrok 4 Fast\n\n...\n\nRouter)\n\n...\n\nol\n\n...\n\nenabled\n\n...\n\nBy default,\n\n...\n\nthe\n\n...\n\nwe wish to\n\n...\n\nI\n\n...\n\nreasoning. We&quot;
./docs/rounds/round-014-grok-1.html:65:  &quot;router_generation_id&quot;: &quot;gen-1786231429-hJpJsn633gMLKnlB0rkp&quot;,
